startup.name: ByteAsk
startup.one_liner: The AI coding agent for C and C++
startup.description: ByteAsk is an AI coding agent for C and C++ that builds, debugs and tests each change with the real compiler, debugger and test suite, runs from terminal and editors, and can be deployed fully on premises. Buyers are teams in trading, automotive, chips and operating systems. Two founders in San Francisco.

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting prior is about 1 percent with a 0.6 to 2 percent band (references/yc_acceptance.md). Up: sharp niche with enterprise buyers who need on prem, technical founders, and a clear technical wedge in verification. Down: general coding agents are improving at C++ and enterprise sales is slow. Known to have been accepted, so completeness only.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly decline because general coding agents from labs and IDE vendors keep improving and can run compilers and tests, so a reviewer would ask why a two person team stays ahead. Open source and on prem claims also raise the question of how it makes money without a long enterprise sales process.

outcomes.why_it_fails: The most likely result is a stall or acquisition by a toolchain or embedded vendor. The niche is real and paid but the market is limited and frontier labs keep closing the quality gap. Even when the company survives, an exit above the cohort median needs revenue growth and a buyer with strategic need, and most acquisitions in the researched set were small and below 100M dollars.

technical_complexity.rationale: Driving real toolchains, debuggers, sanitizers and test suites in sandboxes across build systems is hard to get robust, and large C++ codebases stress context handling. Two strong engineers can build a good agent but breadth of build environments is a long tail.

takeover_risk.rationale: General agents already use toolchains and can be pointed at C++, and vendors have enterprise on prem plans. The niche pays but is small for them, so they may not prioritise it.

evidence.claim: Embedded and automotive coding needs MISRA compliance and toolchain context that generic assistants lack.
Automotive coding assistants are being built, showing demand for C and C++ specific tools.

brand.rationale: The name signals low level programming and asking an assistant. Compound names like Dropbox work, but this one frames the product as a chat Q and A rather than an agent that builds and tests.

narrative.headline: A sharp niche that a seed investor can understand, set against frontier labs that keep improving at the same job.
narrative.general_summary: ByteAsk has a specific buyer (C and C++ teams that need on prem tools) and a specific technical claim (verification with the real toolchain), which is better than a generic coding agent pitch. The cost is a small market and giant competitors. I keep the seed just below the 59 percent B2B anchor because of the very crowded Fall 2026 AI coding field, and the later steps near anchors. The most likely stop is seed or an acquisition by a toolchain vendor. These numbers are anchored on the 2022 to 2025 cohorts, whose later rounds are not yet fully observed, so the true rates are probably somewhat higher than the known only figures and the uncertainty is wide.
